claims.text: The Z method is a computationally efficient alternative to full ab initio thermodynamic integration for high-melting refractory materials.
The Z method can predict melting properties of high-melting refractory materials.
The relevant initial state is a solid high-melting refractory material near its melting point.
The Z method is implemented using ab initio molecular dynamics in a microcanonical constant-energy ensemble.
The simulated solid is superheated until it spontaneously transitions to a liquid.
The spontaneous transition occurs near the thermodynamic melting point.
Solid-liquid interfacial dynamics mediate the transition from the superheated solid to the liquid.
A superheated solid becomes unstable and melts spontaneously in the Z method.
The spontaneous melting transition can be used to infer the melting temperature.
Further analysis of Z-method simulations can determine the entropy and enthalpy of fusion.
Further analysis of Z-method simulations can determine the volume change at melting.
The Z method avoids expensive free-energy integrations.
Z-method melting properties should have accuracy comparable to full free-energy calculations.
The Z method should have significantly lower computational cost than full free-energy calculations.
Traditional ab initio free-energy integration using molecular dynamics is computationally expensive for high-throughput applications.
The Z method may be less accurate for systems with highly complex or anharmonic melting behavior.
Significant finite-size effects may reduce the accuracy of the Z method.

contradictions.description: The intervention specifies a constant-total-energy ensemble, while the mechanism says the same system is gradually heated under constant energy. Gradual energy addition is incompatible with a single microcanonical trajectory unless the text instead means a series of separate simulations initialized at progressively higher energies.
